Passivity
pa-SIV-ih-tee
n. (the state of being acted upon; the refusal to move when the charge says move)
From passive, Latin passivus, capable of suffering or of being acted upon, from pati, to suffer. Webster (1828) marks passivity as little used, and defines it as passiveness: the tendency of a body to persevere in a given state, of motion or of rest, until another body disturbs it. In physics that is inertia. In a man under orders, it is a sin with a scientific name.

Biblical Definition

Passivity is staying as you are when God has already spoken. It is not rest, and it is not meekness. Meekness is strength under control. Passivity is strength that will not engage. Adam was with his wife when she took the fruit, and the text does not record a word from him until the deed was done (Gen 3:6). Aaron made the calf because the people pressed him, and called the resulting feast a feast to the LORD (Exo 32:4-5). Eli heard what his sons did, and his rebuke did not stop them (1Sa 2:22-25). Scripture’s opposite is the command to stand, to watch, to quit you like men (1Co 16:13), and the rebuke of the man who knows his lord’s will and does not do it (Luk 12:47). In this ministry the first letter of R.E.A.L. M.A.N. is Reject Passivity — leading, not waiting. A man who waits to feel ready has already chosen not to move. The body at rest stays at rest until something moves it. A Christian man is not permitted to be that body. God’s command is the force that is meant to move him. Waiting for a more convenient feeling is the drift.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) marks passivity as little used, and defines it as passiveness: the tendency of a body to persevere in a given state, either of motion or of rest, until disturbed by another body.

PASSIV’ITY, noun. Passiveness, which see. [Little used.]

The tendency of a body to persevere in a given state, either of motion or rest, till disturbed by another body.

Key Scripture

1Co 16:13 — "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong."

Jos 1:9 — "Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest."

Neh 6:3 — "And I sent messengers unto them, saying, I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down: why should the work cease, whilst I leave it, and come down to you?"

Jas 4:17 — "Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin."

Modern Corruption

Passivity is now baptized as humility, as “not my place,” and as self-care — so a man can abandon a charge and call the abandonment virtue.

expand to see more

The age has several names for a man who will not move. He is easygoing. He is not controlling. He is giving her space, giving the children room, waiting on God when God has already spoken. Webster’s little-used noun is more honest. A body perseveres in its state until something else disturbs it. That is a law of matter. It is not a law for a steward. The corruption is the decision to treat a moral charge as if it were physics.

The church version is worse, because it borrows true words. Meekness, patience, and submission are virtues. Passivity uses them as cover. Adam’s silence in the garden was not submission to God. Eli’s soft word was not patience. A man rejects passivity when he leads without waiting to be asked, engages when the work is unimpressive, and refuses the story that someone else will handle what was assigned to him. Rest is a gift. Drift is a sin. The two are not neighbors.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin pati, to suffer, to be acted upon. Webster’s noun is physical inertia. Scripture’s indictment is the man who knows the good and does not do it.

expand to see more

Latin passivus, from pati — capable of suffering or of receiving action. The passive man is the man to whom things are done.

Webster (1828) — little used. The tendency to stay in the present state until another body interferes.

Greek mē poieō, in Jas 4:17 — the sin is not a wrong act. It is the good act left undone by the man who knew it.

Greek andrizomai (G407) — quit you like men, act like a man (1Co 16:13). The antonym of passivity is not aggression. It is engaged strength.

Usage

"Passivity is not rest. Rest obeys a command to stop. Passivity ignores a command to move."

"The first letter of R.E.A.L. M.A.N. is Reject Passivity: leading, not waiting to be asked."

"A man who calls his drift humility has renamed a sin with a virtue’s name."
